items.name: RansomEXX
items.model: Ransomware group running targeted, human-operated intrusions
items.summary: The group behind the July 2024 attack on C-Edge Technologies, which knocked nearly 300 Indian co-operative and regional rural banks off UPI and ATM networks. Entry came through a partner's misconfigured Jenkins server. DSCI's March 2026 advisory still lists RansomEXX among the ransomware threats to Indian organisations.
key_findings: C-Edge, a joint venture of SBI and TCS, serves co-operative and regional rural banks. NPCI isolated it from retail payment systems to stop the spread, so customers of nearly 300 small banks lost UPI and ATM access.

CloudSEK attributed the attack to RansomEXX v2.0 and traced the start to a misconfigured Jenkins server at Brontoo Technology Solutions, exploited through the Jenkins CLI file-read flaw CVE-2024-23897.
The banks themselves were not the entry point: a technology partner's internet-facing build server was.
recommended_actions: Take Jenkins and other build servers off the internet, or put them behind VPN and SSO; patch CVE-2024-23897.
Treat vendors with network access as part of your attack surface: inventory their connections and limit them to what they need.
Payment operators: rehearse isolating a service provider quickly, as NPCI did, without taking down every bank.
Keep offline or immutable backups of servers and hypervisors, and test a full restore, not just file recovery.
Put MFA on every VPN, firewall and remote-access login, and remove accounts that are not used.

items.name: LockBit
items.summary: One of the most widely deployed ransomware operations since 2022, with Indian names on its leak site including the brokerage Motilal Oswal, Granules India and the National Aerospace Laboratories. It is still active: Cyble counted 38 LockBit victims in Asia-Pacific in the first half of 2026, and DSCI's 2026 advisory names LockBit 3.0 as a threat to Indian organisations.
key_findings: In February 2024 LockBit listed Motilal Oswal, which serves about six million clients, claiming confidential data. The firm did not confirm or dispute an incident, and CERT-In said it was acting.
TechCrunch lists earlier LockBit attacks on Granules India and India's National Aerospace Laboratories.
Cyble's H1 2026 report places LockBit third in Asia-Pacific with 38 victims, behind The Gentlemen and Qilin.
recommended_actions: Keep offline or immutable backups of servers and hypervisors, and test a full restore, not just file recovery.
Put MFA on every VPN, firewall and remote-access login, and remove accounts that are not used.
Watch for large outbound transfers to cloud storage before encryption: LockBit affiliates steal data first.

items.name: Akira
items.summary: CERT-In warned Indian organisations about Akira in 2023. It claimed the pharmaceutical company Cipla in December 2024, which Cipla has not confirmed, and in 2026 it is still getting in through an old SonicWall SSL VPN flaw.
key_findings: CERT-In's 2023 advisory: Akira deletes Windows shadow copies, appends '.akira' to files and runs double extortion. It spreads through spear-phishing, drive-by downloads and insecure Remote Desktop.
Cyble (August 2026) reports Akira still exploiting CVE-2024-40766 in SonicWall SSL VPN, a patched 2024 flaw.
Akira claimed 70 GB from Cipla in December 2024, including medical, financial and contact data; Cipla has not confirmed it.
recommended_actions: Patch SonicWall SSL VPN for CVE-2024-40766 and rotate VPN credentials that existed before the patch.
Do not expose RDP to the internet.
Keep offline or immutable backups of servers and hypervisors, and test a full restore, not just file recovery.
Put MFA on every VPN, firewall and remote-access login, and remove accounts that are not used.

items.name: The Gentlemen
items.summary: The most active ransomware group in Asia-Pacific in 2026. It emerged in the second half of 2025, probably from affiliates of the Qilin ecosystem, and LevelBlue counted 12 Indian victims among 352 on its leak site by May 2026. It favours exposed VPNs and firewalls and pushes ransomware across a domain through Group Policy.

attack.name: Domain or Tenant Policy Modification: Group Policy Modification

key_findings: Cyble: The Gentlemen led Asia-Pacific in H1 2026 with 114 victims, and again in August 2026 with 20.
LevelBlue (May 2026): 352 leak-site victims from January to 10 May 2026, 12 of them in India. Asia-Pacific was its largest region at 28.7%.

Access comes through exposed remote services, VPN or firewall abuse, stolen credentials and access brokers. Operators use AnyDesk, PsExec, Cobalt Strike and SystemBC, and stage payloads in NETLOGON to deploy them domain-wide through Group Policy.
It encrypts Windows, Linux, NAS, BSD and VMware ESXi, and steals data before encrypting.
recommended_actions: Alert on new or changed Group Policy objects that run executables, and on files written to NETLOGON or SYSVOL.
Allowlist remote-access tools and alert on AnyDesk or PsExec where they are not approved.
Keep offline or immutable backups of servers and hypervisors, and test a full restore, not just file recovery.
Put MFA on every VPN, firewall and remote-access login, and remove accounts that are not used.

items.name: Qilin
items.summary: The most prolific ransomware group in the world in August 2026 with 147 claims, and second in Asia-Pacific in H1 2026. No Indian victim has publicly confirmed a Qilin attack; its place here rests on its regional volume.
key_findings: Cyble: 64 Asia-Pacific victims in H1 2026, second to The Gentlemen; 147 claims worldwide in August 2026, the most of any group.
Qilin is a Russian-speaking operation first seen in 2022 under the name Agenda; affiliates keep 80 to 85% of each ransom.
LevelBlue links The Gentlemen to affiliates from the Qilin ecosystem.
recommended_actions: Keep offline or immutable backups of servers and hypervisors, and test a full restore, not just file recovery.
Put MFA on every VPN, firewall and remote-access login, and remove accounts that are not used.
